Every prior administration allowed some asylum seekers to enter legally at the southwest ports of entry. The Trump administration closed that pathway. The result: legal asylum entries dropped 99.9%, Cato’s @David_J_Bier reports. 

Learn more: ow.ly/Oov850YJ9zT

The Trump administration has likely cut legal immigration more than illegal immigration, says Cato’s @David_J_Bier. The available data suggest that about 2.5 times as many legal entries are being stopped as illegal entries. 

ow.ly/3rZN50YJ9yt

President Trump's executive order directing the USPS not to deliver some lawfully cast ballots oversteps presidential authority. Federal law—not the White House—governs what mail the Postal Service must carry, says Cato’s Walter Olson. 

ow.ly/f34e50YINiH

The updated Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA 2.0) radically expands online privacy rules to teens. But more regulation, even when it claims to protect children, isn’t risk-free, warn Cato’s tech experts. 

ow.ly/hwq650YHiGX

FDA regulations push AI developers away from healthcare's hardest problems. Reforming medical software could let innovators build tools that actually help patients—without years of delay, explain Cato’s Christopher Gardner and @KevinTFrazier. 

ow.ly/4nqb50YJ0nW

Texas's power queue has exploded from 170 GW to over 410 GW in under a year as AI demand surges. Consumer Regulated Electricity would make it more attractive for large consumers to go off-grid —keeping the grid reliable and affordable for everyone, explain Cato’s @ts_fisher and Glen Lyons.

ow.ly/yfiN50YIN5I

The DOJ drafted an analysis on how the US could create a central bank digital currency—then withheld it from the public (and Congress). After 1000+ days, a FOIA request was denied. Cato’s @EconWithNick is suing to force transparency. 

Read more: cato.org/blog/why-im-suing-g…

Federal “equitable sharing” lets police skip state rules meant to protect your property and seize it for profit, but Nevada's legislature never authorized it. The state’s supreme court should let Nevada enforce its own property protections, argues Cato’s Matthew Cavedon.

ow.ly/Ggil50YIqFM

Tax Day is here — but how well do you really know the US tax system? 

Cato's @adamnmichel breaks down five things that might change how you think about it.

Video

Most affordability proposals in Washington and state capitals flunk basic economics, says Cato’s @MrRBourne. They mainly just reshuffle the burden and paper over the real industry-specific drivers of high prices. 

On April 16, we are releasing the Cato “Handbook on Affordability,” featuring 100+ policy ideas to defuse inflation and lower the cost of living.

Average American workers pay low taxes compared to those in EU countries, Cato’s @adamnmichel and @SantiagoForster report.

Belgium, Germany, Austria, France, and Italy confiscate more than half of their workers’ pretax compensation. An average US worker sends less than a third of their income to the government. 
 
ow.ly/Aw1T50YHiqv

The Fed and politicians in Congress caused the affordability crisis. Now politicians want to compound the error by fixing prices, increasing subsidies, and instituting new mandates. This isn’t a sustainable route to lowering living costs. It’s a recipe for more chaos.

Video

The rich pay the highest tax rates in the United States. The top 10% of income earners pay more than 60% of all federal taxes and 72% of income taxes, Cato’s @adamnmichel and @SantiagoForster explain.

ow.ly/eee850YHimG

Stung by groceries, electricity, and used car prices being almost 30% or more higher than in 2020, Americans now equate high prices with a poor economy. Politicians want to impose sector-by-sector interventions to provide relief. But most affordability proposals flunk basic economics, explains Cato’s @MrRBourne. 

On April 16, we are releasing the Cato “Handbook on Affordability,” featuring 100+ policy ideas to defuse inflation and lower the cost of living.

The 25th Amendment isn’t a tool for dealing with a controversial president—it’s a last resort for when a president cannot carry out the duties of the office. Urging the vice president to invoke it distracts from Congress’s existing power to check the president, says Cato’s Molly Nixon.

ow.ly/AJJF50YIo2R

US aluminum tariffs were supposed to boost security. Instead, they raised prices, hurt manufacturers, and pushed reliable Canadian producers away. With US smelters still closing and the Iran war denting supplies, the US is more vulnerable—not less. A policy own goal, explains Cato’s @scottlincicome.

ow.ly/G1Jx50YIbOs

Hungary tried national conservatism. The result: a lagging economy, rampant corruption, and a declining birth rate. Voters just delivered the verdict. Cato’s @johanknorberg explains what it means—and why it matters far beyond Hungary.

Video

Supporters said the Inflation Reduction Act would make Medicare drugs more affordable. Instead, CBO just raised its 10-year Medicare Part D spending projection by $600 billion. Cato scholar @mfcannon explains why government cost controls keep backfiring.

ow.ly/t2Ka50YHhV4

America’s electric power grid can’t keep up with demand. A new idea—Consumer-Regulated Electricity—would allow private, permissionless grids to expand energy faster and more efficiently, says Cato’s @ts_fisher.

Video

What can life on the front lines of criminal justice teach us about American law today? Join @RandyEBarnett for a discussion of his new memoir, Felony Review: Tales of True Crime and Corruption in Chicago, a gripping account of his years as a young prosecutor in the Cook County State’s Attorney’s Office in the late 1970s and early ’80s.

Register: ow.ly/iS2Y50YHctQ
